title: Meet The Woggels!

jokes.text: The TGS sweatshirts were supposed to say 'TGS Season Six, Yuck,' which is a catch-phrase from a pretty great sketch. But they got misprinted and now they say 'TGS Season Six, Duck!' And that's a season five catchphrase.
jokes.setup: Liz has a 'huge problem' — misprinted sweatshirts
jokes.punchline: The problem is not the misprint itself but that 'Duck!' is last season's catchphrase — an absurdly hyperspecific, self-serious complaint about something utterly trivial
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon opening — she presents something utterly inconsequential as a catastrophe, and the joke deepens as you realize the 'real' problem is catchphrase anachronism. Strong character integration because only someone as myopically TGS-obsessed as Liz would care about this distinction.

jokes.text: A real problem is losing your giant scissors right before a ribbon-cutting for a couch factory. I just...had them.
jokes.setup: Jack dismisses Liz's sweatshirt crisis as not a 'real problem'
jokes.punchline: His real problem is also absurd — giant scissors — delivered with complete sincerity and the confused afterthought 'I just...had them'
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Jack's pompous dismissal is itself absurd because his 'real' problem is equally silly (giant ceremonial scissors), and the trailing 'I just...had them' sells genuine bewilderment. Economy is excellent — no wasted words. Strong Jack character integration: he takes ceremonial capitalism trappings completely seriously.

jokes.text: Factories provide three things this country desperately needs: Jobs, pride, and material for Bruce Springsteen songs.
jokes.setup: Jack earnestly lists what factories provide America
jokes.punchline: The third item — 'material for Bruce Springsteen songs' — subverts the sincere patriotic list with an absurd specificity
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect list joke structure: two sincere items, one absurd subversion. The Springsteen reference is earned because it's genuinely culturally accurate (he DOES write about factory towns) while being a ridiculous thing to list as a national need. The economy is exceptional — maximum laughs per word. One of the tightest jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Great, so we solved your problem, but now I've gotta wear last year's sweatshirt to my cousin's wedding.
jokes.setup: Jack's scissors are found and his problem is solved
jokes.punchline: Liz's concern immediately pivots back to herself — wearing a TGS sweatshirt to a wedding is already absurd, but it being 'last year's' is the kicker
jokes.explanation: Solid callback that pays off the opening joke — the sweatshirt is still Liz's problem, and the absurdity of wearing ANY TGS sweatshirt to a wedding is understated perfectly. Good character integration (Liz's obliviousness to social norms).

jokes.text: Oh, I listened to rock and roll music once, but I stopped before I started worshipping the devil. The song went, 'Mr. Sandma--', then I shut it off.
jokes.setup: Jenna mentions her rock star boyfriend
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's religious paranoia is so extreme that he stopped listening to 'Mr. Sandman' — an utterly wholesome song — before the first syllable of 'man,' fearing devil worship
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Kenneth joke. The specificity of 'Mr. Sandma--' is genius — the joke lives in the hyphen, the moment he cut himself off. It's not just that he's fearful of rock music (that's the expected Kenneth beat), it's the specific absurdity of choosing the most innocent possible song and still finding it dangerous. Perfect character integration — no other character on TV could deliver this. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Back in Chicago, I walked in on you with the guy from Blues Traveler. He still had his harmonica thing on.
jokes.setup: Liz challenges Jenna's claim that dating a musician is new for her
jokes.punchline: The specificity of Blues Traveler (a second-tier band) and the detail that he 'still had his harmonica thing on' (the Hohner harness) paints a vivid, absurd image
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Blues Traveler' is funny on its own — why Blues Traveler? — but 'he still had his harmonica thing on' elevates it significantly. The detail makes you picture the exact scenario and it's very funny. Good use of specificity as a comedy tool.

jokes.text: Like Yoko Ono and the Beatles, or Lance Drake Mandrell and Wilson Phillips.
jokes.setup: Jenna explains she wants to sexually manipulate a musician into leaving his band
jokes.punchline: She pairs the famous Yoko/Beatles reference with a completely invented, absurdist fake-famous equivalent: 'Lance Drake Mandrell and Wilson Phillips'
jokes.explanation: Brilliant construction: it starts with a real, recognizable reference (Yoko/Beatles), then pairs it with a fabricated parallel that sounds just plausible enough ('Lance Drake Mandrell' mixing Lance Bass + Barbara Mandrell sound, 'Wilson Phillips' as a real but lesser group). The fake name is crafted to sound authentically show-biz. Classic 30 Rock — the joke rewards people who notice the absurdity.

jokes.text: They sold out Madison Square Garden in nine minutes, for a Tuesday morning show.
jokes.setup: Jenna brags about her boyfriend's band's popularity
jokes.punchline: The impressive sell-out speed is immediately undermined by 'for a Tuesday morning show' — children's concerts happen on weekday mornings, which makes it much less impressive
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection structure — you're set up to be impressed by the sell-out, then the Tuesday morning detail deflates it perfectly. The economy is tight; everything lands in the last clause.

jokes.text: Wait, who plays on a Tuesday morning? / I don't know, just a little band called the Woggels.
jokes.setup: The obvious question about Tuesday morning shows sets up a reveal
jokes.punchline: 'Just a little band called the Woggels' delivered with the same gravitas one would use for 'just a little band called the Rolling Stones' — the absurdity of treating a children's band this way
jokes.explanation: Works as a setup for the Woggels reveal, with Jenna's self-seriousness being the joke — she delivers 'the Woggels' with full drama. The song that follows immediately confirms and amplifies the absurdity.

jokes.text: ♪ Apples are red / bananas are yellow / I love my friends, bananas are yellow ♪ — The Woggels' song lyrics
jokes.setup: Jenna has been building up her rock star boyfriend's band as hugely successful
jokes.punchline: The actual music is infantile nonsense — 'bananas are yellow' repeated, with the song structure collapsing mid-lyric
jokes.explanation: The payoff for the Woggels setup is the actual music, which perfectly parodies children's songs — repetitive, nonsensical, and completely sincere. 'I love my friends, bananas are yellow' repeating the wrong line is a great touch showing the genre's low bar.

jokes.text: My Russ is the blue one. He's about to do something amazing.
jokes.setup: Jenna watches the Woggels with pride
jokes.punchline: Referring to a children's entertainer by costume color ('the blue one') while anticipating something 'amazing' from a toddler show is deeply incongruous with her usual self-seriousness
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Jenna's complete earnestness about her Woggel boyfriend is funny, and 'the blue one' nails how children's entertainers are identified. Not outstanding but works in context.

jokes.text: Oh, I know the Woggels. My eight-year-old niece walked down the aisle to that song at her wedding.
jokes.setup: Liz says she knows the Woggels
jokes.punchline: Her eight-year-old niece had a WEDDING — with no acknowledgment of how disturbing this is — and the absurdity is played completely straight
jokes.explanation: Exceptional sleeper joke. The Woggels recognition is just a setup — the real bomb is 'eight-year-old niece...at her wedding,' dropped with zero fanfare. The character integration works because Liz says this like it's completely normal, suggesting her family is genuinely chaotic. The economy is perfect — the horror is delivered in a subordinate clause.

jokes.text: Well, it ticks off a lot of boxes on my sexual walkabout list. 'Yoko a band, make love to a beloved children's entertainer, be with a non-aboriginal Australian--'
jokes.setup: Someone asks why Jenna wants to break up a children's group
jokes.punchline: She has a literal 'sexual walkabout list' with specific, escalating categories — 'non-aboriginal Australian' as a category is particularly absurd
jokes.explanation: The 'sexual walkabout list' is a great Jenna concept — her sexual adventures are so systematic she has a spreadsheet. Each list item escalates absurdly: 'Yoko a band' (already odd), 'children's entertainer' (worse), 'non-aboriginal Australian' (weirdly specific racial/ethnic carve-out that tells you a lot about Jenna). Strong character specificity.

jokes.text: Maybe Raffi. Or the sedated prisoner they put inside of Barney.
jokes.setup: Jenna hopes Paul is also with a beloved children's entertainer
jokes.punchline: After mentioning Raffi, she adds 'the sedated prisoner they put inside of Barney' — a deeply dark, conspiracy-theory-inflected take on the Barney costume
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'The sedated prisoner they put inside of Barney' is a perfect dark-absurdist construction — it implies an entire world of grimness (someone is being forced, while sedated, to inhabit the Barney suit as punishment) without explaining any of it. The specificity of 'sedated' is doing heavy comedic lifting. Extremely quotable, and rewards rewatching because it's so casually dropped. Close to the caliber of the anchor examples.

jokes.text: Something terrible has happened! And for once I'm not talking about the collapse of the middle class.
jokes.setup: Tracy bursts in dramatically announcing something terrible
jokes.punchline: The clarification that he's NOT talking about the middle class collapse implies he regularly storms in about macroeconomic trends — absurd for Tracy — and raises the stakes on what his actual problem is
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Tracy line. It's funny because Tracy is the LAST person you'd expect to be concerned about the middle class, making the implied backstory very funny. The structure is perfect: the dramatic opener, then the subversive clarification. The economy is flawless — two sentences do a lot of work. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: My oldest son, George Foreman, got into Stanford.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces his terrible problem
jokes.punchline: His son is named 'George Foreman' — after the boxer/grill entrepreneur — played completely straight
jokes.explanation: A classic 30 Rock background joke delivered as a throwaway. The name 'George Foreman' for Tracy's son is perfectly in character (Tracy's chaotic celebrity-obsessed world) and is played with no wink — you have to catch it yourself. The economy is perfect because it's just casually stated.

jokes.text: Tracy, that's awesome. Stanford's a great school. I didn't even get in, and I was first in my class. Although, only seven of us graduated that year because of a bad mono outbreak which somehow missed me, despite all the frenching I did.
jokes.setup: Dotcom praises Stanford
jokes.punchline: His qualification of being 'first in his class' crumbles as he reveals only 7 graduated due to mono — and then the absurd self-incrimination: he avoided mono despite extensive 'frenching'
jokes.explanation: Great Dotcom joke that uses his 'underutilized intellectual' characterization well. It escalates perfectly: legitimate brag → undermined by small class size → undermined further by disease → self-incriminating detail about 'all the frenching.' Each beat lands. 'Despite all the frenching I did' is the money line.

jokes.text: Jordan men don't go to college. We go to the school of hard knocks, a one-year vocational program where you learn to bang on doors and scare people into subscribing to magazines that they'll never get.
jokes.setup: Tracy objects to his son going to college on principle
jokes.punchline: 'School of hard knocks' is taken literally and given an absurdly specific, depressing curriculum — scam magazine subscriptions
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Taking the cliché 'school of hard knocks' literally and defining it as a '1-year vocational program' in magazine subscription scamming is inspired. The joke implies Tracy went to this school himself, which explains everything. The specificity of the scam (door-to-door, subscriptions never delivered) is perfect — it's a real recognizable fraud, not a random one.

jokes.text: Really, Dotcom? How did your city council campaign go? / Well, as far as raising the level of discourse in this city? I'd say it was a great success.
jokes.setup: Dotcom insists Tracy should be proud of George Foreman's academic success
jokes.punchline: Tracy's dismissive callback to Dotcom's failed city council run, and Dotcom's dignified spin on the loss ('raising the level of discourse') while clearly having lost badly
jokes.explanation: Good exchange. Tracy's ruthless dismissal is funny, but Dotcom's diplomatic self-delusion about the campaign's legacy is the real joke — he lost but has reframed it as a moral victory. Good character work for both.

jokes.text: This is Angie's fault! She coddled him. I'm gonna teach my son what it is to be a Jordan. And I'm gonna die trying!
jokes.setup: Tracy resolves to toughen up his son
jokes.punchline: 'And I'm gonna die trying!' — a misapplication of the idiom 'I'll die trying' that makes his parenting mission sound like a fatal combat mission, inadvertently suggesting Tracy knows he's dangerous
jokes.explanation: Tracy's dramatic exit line plays well because it accidentally foreshadows how chaotic his 'teaching' will be. The 'die trying' framing is funnier than standard because it implies mutual danger.

jokes.text: Born April 24, 1925, at Boston Catholic Guilt Hospital.
jokes.setup: The doctor reads off Colleen's details to confirm her identity
jokes.punchline: 'Boston Catholic Guilt Hospital' — a real-sounding hospital name that encapsulates everything about Colleen's personality and Jack's upbringing
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Boston Catholic Guilt Hospital' is a perfect compressed joke — it sounds plausible as a real hospital (Boston has many Catholic hospitals) while cramming an entire character study of Colleen and the Donaghy family dynamic into four words. The economy is flawless. It's both a great standalone joke and richly character-specific. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: She keeps calling me Aladdin. / That's definitely her.
jokes.setup: Dr. Singh (presumably South Asian) describes the patient calling him Aladdin
jokes.punchline: Jack's instant recognition — 'that's definitely her' — confirms Colleen is casually racist, and Jack is so used to it he identifies her by this trait
jokes.explanation: Tight two-line exchange. The joke is that Jack not only isn't surprised by his mother's racism but uses it as a reliable identifier. The deadpan delivery implied in 'that's definitely her' is perfect. Dark but earns it through character consistency with Colleen's established personality.

jokes.text: We found your name on a list of disappointments she keeps folded up in her shoe.
jokes.setup: The doctor explains how they found Jack's contact information
jokes.punchline: Colleen keeps a 'list of disappointments' — in her shoe — and Jack is on it. The specificity of 'in her shoe' makes it significantly funnier.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. Everything about it works: the category ('list of disappointments'), the medium (a physical list, not mental), the location ('in her shoe' — why her shoe?), and the implication that Jack is on it. The shoe detail transforms a good joke into a great one because it suggests obsessive, well-worn grievance. Highly quotable and character-defining for Colleen.

jokes.text: Dr. Singh, are you stealing my hats? What do you do, feed them to your cow God?
jokes.setup: Jack gets Colleen on the phone and she immediately attacks the doctor
jokes.punchline: Colleen accuses the Indian doctor of both hat theft and feeding them to a Hindu deity — two racist non-sequiturs delivered in rapid succession
jokes.explanation: Colleen's racist outbursts are a series staple and this one is in character. The 'cow God' detail is specific enough to be funny (she's not entirely wrong about Hindu sacred cows, making it more absurd). Works as character comedy more than as a crafted joke structure.

jokes.text: Somebody got all flouncy when I wasn't looking. What are you gonna do, put on your galoshes and go eat some fruit, like a Frenchman?
jokes.setup: Jack mentions he's opening a sofa factory
jokes.punchline: Colleen's attack on sofas/furniture as French effeminacy — the specific image of galoshes + fruit = Frenchman is absurdly specific and bizarre
jokes.explanation: 'Galoshes + fruit = Frenchman' is a wonderful Colleen absurdism. The chain of logic (sofa → comfort → softness → France) is exactly how her mind works, and the specific accessories she assigns to Frenchmen are both wrong and very funny. 'Flouncy' is a great word choice. Strong Colleen voice.

jokes.text: There's only one reason I came to New York, and that's because Gunga Din here takes my insurance.
jokes.setup: Colleen is asked why she's in New York
jokes.punchline: She insults the Indian doctor with 'Gunga Din' (a racist reference to the 1939 film) while claiming purely financial motives for her visit — both the racism and the denial are simultaneously the joke
jokes.explanation: Colleen's deflection ('it's just insurance') is the real joke — the audience knows she's there for Jack — but the 'Gunga Din' reference shows the depth of her period-specific racism. The dual-layer works well.

jokes.text: My good friend Dick Cheney got one. A month later, he and I went hunting in Mexico. He shot thousands of doves that day and only hit me in the leg once.
jokes.setup: Jack shows familiarity with the LVAD heart device
jokes.punchline: Reference to Cheney's infamous hunting accident — but Jack has inverted it: thousands of doves, only one leg hit, presented as a positive ratio
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jack joke. The Cheney hunting incident reference is well-chosen because it's a specific real event. But the twist is Jack being the one shot, and framing 'only hit me in the leg once' as a good outcome reveals both his loyalty to powerful men and his masochistic GOP-insider worldview. The word 'only' is doing a lot of work. Very quotable.

jokes.text: ♪ Basketballs hula hoops rollercoaster loop-the-loops / you just heard the Woggels sing / a very silly list of things ♪ — Woggels mid-song
jokes.setup: The Woggels continue performing their children's show
jokes.punchline: The song's lyrics include a line explicitly stating what the song is ('you just heard the Woggels sing a very silly list of things') — a children's song that meta-describes itself mid-performance
jokes.explanation: Good continuation of the Woggels absurdism. The meta-lyric ('you just heard the Woggels sing a very silly list of things') parodies how children's songs often describe what they're doing mid-song. The Woggels' particular brand of low-ambition music is consistently funny.

jokes.text: Like the flashlight in my race war preparedness bag.
jokes.setup: The doctor mentions the LVAD runs on rechargeable batteries
jokes.punchline: Jack's frame of reference for rechargeable batteries is his 'race war preparedness bag' — a darkly comic window into Jack's paranoid conservative worldview
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Race war preparedness bag' is a perfect Jack Donaghy detail — not a normal 'go bag' or 'emergency kit' but specifically a RACE WAR bag, implying Jack has thought through this scenario carefully. The economy is unmatched — it's a single prepositional phrase that tells you everything. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: What good would he have been? He's useless in a hospital. I recall this one time he cried and cried. I mean, it was more like wailing. It was awful. / She's referring to my birth.
jokes.setup: Colleen explains why she didn't call Jack
jokes.punchline: Her story about his worst hospital behavior turns out to be his birth — and his understated clarification 'she's referring to my birth' lands perfectly
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed. Colleen's escalating complaint about Jack's hospital behavior (crying → wailing → 'it was awful') builds genuine misdirection — you might think she means a recent incident. The payoff 'she's referring to my birth' combined with his matter-of-fact tone is devastating. The joke reveals their whole relationship: Colleen was annoyed by Jack from the moment he existed. Masterclass in structure and character integration.

jokes.text: This is supposed to be a hospital, not a Japanese internment camp I volunteered at during the war.
jokes.setup: Colleen complains about her hospital room
jokes.punchline: She compares it to a Japanese internment camp — which she VOLUNTEERED AT — implying she chose to work in one, which is significantly darker than just knowing about them
jokes.explanation: 'I volunteered at during the war' is the essential word choice — not 'visited' or 'heard about' but actively volunteered to work at. The implication that young Colleen participated in one of America's worst civil rights violations as a volunteer activity is very dark and very funny. Perfect Colleen characterization — she is not on the right side of history.

jokes.text: You could look out at the park and watch carriage horses being whipped. I know how you love that.
jokes.setup: Jack offers to put Colleen up at the Plaza
jokes.punchline: Jack sells the Plaza by mentioning she can watch horses being whipped — presenting this as a known preference of hers
jokes.explanation: Good Colleen-via-Jack joke. The specificity of 'horse whipping' as her known pleasure is dark but in keeping with her cruel character. 'I know how you love that' confirms it's not just a general perk but a tailored Colleen amenity. Works well.

jokes.text: I can't go to the Plaza, and you know it. What if I run into Eloise? Am I supposed not to mention the fact that she has a gay grandson? Everybody knows!
jokes.setup: Jack suggests the Plaza as an alternative
jokes.punchline: Colleen's objection is that she'd have to confront the fictional character Eloise (from the children's books set at the Plaza) about her gay grandson — treating a fictional character as a real social acquaintance
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke on multiple levels. First: Colleen treats the fictional Eloise as a real Plaza resident she knows socially. Second: she's preoccupied with Eloise's gay grandson (a fabricated detail — Eloise has no canonical grandson). Third: 'Everybody knows!' implies this is an open secret in her social circle about a fictional child's fictional grandchild. The layers of absurdity are perfectly stacked and the Eloise reference is unexpected and specific. One of the best in the episode.

jokes.text: Because at Ellis Island, your mother's name was recorded as 'unclaimed Irish stowaway.'
jokes.setup: Colleen asks why Jack didn't name Liddy after her mother
jokes.punchline: Her mother's official Ellis Island name was literally 'unclaimed Irish stowaway' — a bureaucratic designation that tells a whole story of immigrant poverty and family chaos
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest jokes in the episode. 'Unclaimed Irish stowaway' as a legal name is both very funny and historically resonant — it implies the entire Donaghy family line literally started with an anonymous, abandoned immigrant child. The joke tells a whole backstory in five words and is perfectly Jack: he delivers dark family history as a casual conversation-ender. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Son, we have a lot of work to do today if I'm gonna 'reverse Urkel' you.
jokes.setup: Tracy wants to toughen up his bookish son
jokes.punchline: 'Reverse Urkel' as a parenting philosophy — taking someone from nerdy to streetwise, the opposite of Steve Urkel's trajectory
jokes.explanation: 'Reverse Urkel' is a great coingage — immediately understandable (Urkel as the ur-nerd), applied to child-rearing with complete seriousness by Tracy. The economy of the phrase is excellent. Perfectly Tracy — he has a pop-cultural framework for everything.

jokes.text: Jordan men don't read. Grizz, tear this book in half.
jokes.setup: George Foreman says he just wants to read
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response is to have Grizz physically destroy the book — the escalation from 'don't read' to immediate book destruction is fast and absurd
jokes.explanation: Good escalation — going from 'don't read' to immediate physical book-destruction is classic Tracy overreaction. The brevity sells it: three words of explanation, then immediate action. Strong Tracy voice.

jokes.text: It's montage time. / Tray, montage got married and quit stripping.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces a training montage
jokes.punchline: Grizz's response treats 'Montage' as a person (a stripper named Montage) who has since settled down — a surreal piece of world-building that treats a film trope as literal person
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. 'Montage got married and quit stripping' is a masterpiece of meta-comedy. It takes a film trope (the montage), personifies it as a strip club employee named Montage, and then gives her a character arc (she got married, left the industry). The joke operates on three levels simultaneously: meta-commentary on montage conventions, absurdist character comedy (Tracy/Grizz know a stripper named Montage), and the warm specificity of 'quit stripping' implying a normal life. Could only exist in 30 Rock. Comparable to the highest-tier anchor examples in originality and construction.

jokes.text: Lemon, my mother did explain sex to me, three years ago. There were... drawings.
jokes.setup: Liz mentions 'the talk' and Jack misunderstands it as the sex talk
jokes.punchline: Colleen explained sex to Jack when he was in his 50s (she'd have been in her 80s) and used drawings — implying she waited until late in life and made it a formal illustrated presentation
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The pause before 'There were... drawings' is perfect — you hear Jack slightly traumatized by the memory. The comedy comes from: (1) the age at which this happened (Jack is well into adulthood), (2) Colleen creating visual aids, and (3) Jack's pained understatement. Very quotable and deeply character-specific to both Jack and Colleen.

jokes.text: You talk in your sleep. I know what you did in the war, and before you die, I want you to know that I know.
jokes.setup: Liz talks about having difficult conversations before it's too late
jokes.punchline: Liz reveals she has learned Jack's wartime secrets from sleep-talking and frames it as something she needs him to know she knows — suggesting both intimacy and mutual accountability
jokes.explanation: Good dark joke. The implications are vast — what exactly did Jack do in the war? The comedy is in the gravity Liz assigns to this (which is both funny and oddly touching) and the absurdity of sleep-talking as her intel source. The repeated 'I know that I know' structure is excellent.

jokes.text: There was no need for us to start jabbering about our feelings and sobbing like Bill Belichick listening to Adele.
jokes.setup: Jack dismisses the need for emotional conversations with his mother
jokes.punchline: Bill Belichick — the notoriously stoic, emotionless NFL coach — secretly sobbing to Adele is a perfect absurdist celebrity pairing
jokes.explanation: Brilliant simile. Belichick is the perfect avatar for emotional suppression (famous for his cold press conference demeanor), and pairing him with Adele (whose music is designed to make you cry) creates a perfect incongruity. The joke implies Jack has seen or imagined this, which is an extra layer of absurdity. Very quotable.

jokes.text: As my coffee cup said this morning, 'you only regret the things you didn't do. This cup was made from recycled toilet paper.'
jokes.setup: Jack quotes inspirational wisdom from his coffee cup
jokes.punchline: The inspirational message is immediately followed by the cup's recycled toilet paper disclosure — the juxtaposition of profound and disgusting on the same object
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. The setup leads you to expect more inspirational content or Jack's ironic response to it, then pivots to the sanitary concern about what he's drinking from. The mundane recycling disclosure after the lofty quote is well-timed. The joke also works as a meta-comment on corporate wellness culture.

jokes.text: Last word. / Damn it!
jokes.setup: Jack tries to end the conversation decisively
jokes.punchline: Liz gets the last word by saying 'last word,' and Jack — the man who always wins — is defeated by this simple trick and knows it
jokes.explanation: Fast and efficient. The comedy is in Jack's loss of control in the smallest possible arena — and his 'Damn it!' confirming he walked right into it. The economy is perfect (four words total) and the character dynamic (Liz defeating Jack with childish tactics) is consistently funny throughout the series.

jokes.text: It's good. It's really good. And this is coming from someone Quincy Jones once pushed off a boat.
jokes.setup: Jenna praises Russ's song
jokes.punchline: She validates her music credentials by citing being pushed off a boat by Quincy Jones — implying she knows him well enough for a hostile boating incident
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jenna joke. Being pushed off a boat by Quincy Jones is a perfect celebrity anecdote — specific enough to feel real, bizarre enough to be entirely fictional, and strangely specific (why a boat? why Quincy Jones?). Jenna's use of it as a musical credential is perfectly delusional. The economy is great — it's entirely a subordinate clause. Very quotable.

jokes.text: It doesn't matter what this brain thinks. It matters what this brain thinks.
jokes.setup: Jenna tells Russ his opinion of his own music matters
jokes.punchline: She gestures first to her head, then to somewhere else (implied: her heart, or more likely a lower body part) — the visual gag depends on the second gesture being absurd
jokes.explanation: This is primarily a visual joke — the transcript gives us both 'this brain' references but not what she's pointing to on the second one. Works as Jenna character comedy (probably pointing to something inappropriate) but loses some impact in transcript form. Rewatch bonus for visual payoff.

jokes.text: She won't go to a hotel, and she hates the Princeton Club, because Dean Cain is always there hoping to get recognized.
jokes.setup: Jack lists places his mother refuses to stay
jokes.punchline: Dean Cain (Superman actor, now D-list celebrity) haunts the Princeton Club hoping to be recognized — and Colleen finds this annoying, not endearing
jokes.explanation: Good celebrity specificity joke. Dean Cain is the perfect choice — just famous enough to be recognizable, just obscure enough to make his vigil at the Princeton Club sad. The detail 'hoping to get recognized' is both specific and universal celebrity-ego commentary.

jokes.text: I tried to leave her at the 'Bodies' exhibit.
jokes.setup: Jack lists places he tried to leave Colleen
jokes.punchline: Attempting to abandon your 87-year-old post-surgical mother at a display of preserved human corpses is dark and specific
jokes.explanation: Short and dark. 'Bodies' exhibit as a dumping ground for Colleen is grimly appropriate — she'd fit right in, both aesthetically (old, possibly dessicated) and because Jack is tired of her. Economy is excellent — just one clause.

jokes.text: I decided something last night after I got your tenth text message, one of which was an inscrutable emoticon. Hold it sideways, it's me going like this: 'Talk to your mother!' The '8' is my glasses.
jokes.setup: Jack received many texts from Liz about Colleen
jokes.punchline: Liz has created an emoticon face where the '8' represents her thick glasses — described and presumably demonstrated physically — a deeply Liz form of technological communication
jokes.explanation: Good Liz character joke. The emoticon with '8' for glasses is exactly how Liz communicates — earnestly, slightly off-trend, requiring explanation. The detail that it's 'inscrutable' until explained is the key beat. Rewatch bonus for seeing Liz demonstrate the face.

jokes.text: Well, your way is wrong, and I bet Colleen agrees with me. / I'm glad you said that, Lemon. Good luck.
jokes.setup: Liz insists she can convince Colleen to have the emotional talk
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately sends her in alone with Colleen — 'good luck' delivered with the satisfaction of a man setting someone up to fail
jokes.explanation: Good Jack beat. His 'I'm glad you said that' followed by 'good luck' is the move of someone delighted to see Liz walk into the lion's den. The setup-and-abandon structure works well for the Jack/Liz dynamic.

jokes.text: Can we do something about the temperature in here? I'd like it humid and cold.
jokes.setup: Liz enters Colleen's hospital room
jokes.punchline: Colleen's ideal climate is 'humid and cold' — the most unpleasant possible combination, chosen apparently for preference, not necessity
jokes.explanation: 'Humid and cold' as a preferred climate is perfectly Colleen — it's the worst of both worlds, chosen with absolute conviction. Perfect economy (four words, complete character sketch) and strong character integration.

jokes.text: Duck! [Colleen's reaction to the word]
jokes.setup: Liz has been carrying the 'Duck!' catchphrase from the sweatshirt subplot
jokes.punchline: Colleen instinctively ducks at the word 'Duck!' — the callback to the opening TGS catchphrase joke lands in a completely different context
jokes.explanation: The callback lands because it's organic — Colleen ducks because she thinks someone literally said 'duck' (as in, something is coming). The TGS catchphrase finally has an in-world effect. The context shift makes the callback funnier than the original joke.

jokes.text: In Australia, 'woggel' means 'white.'
jokes.setup: Ian invokes 'Woggel power' to convince Russ to stay.
jokes.punchline: The band name itself means 'white' in Australia — a children's band built on accidental (or intentional) racial terminology.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly timed revelation. 'Woggel means white' reframes the entire children's band concept as accidentally (or deliberately) racially charged — and delivered as the 'except for the shark' justification moment passes. Great dark subversion.

jokes.text: Yoko announcement. Russ wrote a song. A great song. And if you don't sing it at the Gwammys, which is the Grammys for toddlers, Russ is going solo.
jokes.setup: Jenna confronts the Woggels on behalf of Russ
jokes.punchline: 'The Gwammys, which is the Grammys for toddlers' — the Woggels have their own awards show called the Gwammys, with a toddler-speech mispronunciation baked into the name
jokes.explanation: Excellent world-building joke. 'Gwammys' is a perfect name for the children's entertainment Grammys — it mimics how toddlers mispronounce 'Grammys,' so the award show's name is itself a children's version of the word. The self-explanation ('which is the Grammys for toddlers') is necessary but delivered perfectly by Jenna as a solemn announcement. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Except for the shark that got a hold of the fifth Woggel.
jokes.setup: Ian insists nothing can tear the Woggels apart
jokes.punchline: Apparently a shark DID tear them apart — it ate the fifth member, a fact revealed as a casual historical footnote
jokes.explanation: Exceptional construction. The declaration 'nothing can tear us apart' immediately self-refutes with a shark fatality. The bathos is perfect — a children's entertainer was eaten by a shark, and this is just acknowledged matter-of-factly mid-speech. 'Got a hold of' as the verb choice (rather than 'killed' or 'ate') adds to the casual horror. One of the best jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Don't you think, at a certain point in life, parents and children should sit down and express their feelings before it's too late? / God on a wheel!
jokes.setup: Liz attempts to broach the emotional conversation with Colleen
jokes.punchline: 'God on a wheel!' — Colleen's expletive is a period-specific religious oath that manages to be both blasphemous and extremely old-fashioned
jokes.explanation: 'God on a wheel!' is a perfect Colleen exclamation — archaic, vaguely blasphemous, entirely distinct from any modern swearing. It implies a torture-device image (the breaking wheel) which makes it darker than 'God in heaven.' Exclusively Colleen vocabulary. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Jackie and I know how we feel. We don't have to say it out loud like a couple of gays getting married in jean shorts in Provincetown while I'm just trying to enjoy an ice cream on the pier!
jokes.setup: Colleen refuses to express feelings out loud
jokes.punchline: Her objection to emotional expression is framed through a very specific, vivid homophobic scenario involving jean shorts, Provincetown pier, and interrupted ice cream — the specificity suggests this is a real memory
jokes.explanation: Excellent Colleen speech. The complaint is structured perfectly — she begins with the refusal, then expands into an inexplicably detailed scenario that clearly happened to her. 'While I'm just trying to enjoy an ice cream on the pier' as the victim of gay visibility is a masterful touch. The specificity (jean shorts, Provincetown, pier, ice cream) elevates it from a generic bigotry joke to a very specific personal grudge. Very quotable and rewatchable.

jokes.text: Maybe you'll listen to the words of Mike and the Mechanics, whose song The Living Years I definitely remember.
jokes.setup: Liz pivots to citing a song to make her argument about parent-child communication
jokes.punchline: 'Whose song The Living Years I definitely remember' — the qualifier 'I definitely remember' immediately signals she does NOT remember it and is about to fumble the lyrics
jokes.explanation: Excellent setup for the following joke. 'I definitely remember' is a perfect tell — the overconfidence immediately signals failure. The specific choice of Mike and the Mechanics is also funny because they're a real but obscure enough band that misremembering is plausible.

jokes.text: 'Say it out, speak it clear. You should listen, dude. Also, hear. It's too late, when--'
jokes.setup: Liz confidently quotes The Living Years
jokes.punchline: Her 'lyrics' are hilariously mangled — 'you should listen, dude. Also, hear.' — before she's cut off, confirming she remembered nothing
jokes.explanation: Great payoff to the setup. The fake lyrics are perfect: they capture the emotional intent of the real song ('say it out loud, communicate') while being hilariously generic and poorly constructed ('you should listen, dude. Also, hear.'). 'Dude' as a lyric is the perfect wrong note. The interruption before she finishes is ideal timing.

jokes.text: You have two minutes to find that battery before I die.
jokes.setup: Colleen has been ignoring Liz's emotional appeal; presumably her LVAD battery has died
jokes.punchline: Colleen shuts down the entire emotional conversation by announcing she will literally die in two minutes if the battery isn't found — treating her own imminent death as a convenient topic-ender
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Colleen using her own potential death as a conversation escape is perfect characterization — she'd literally rather die than discuss feelings. The delivery implied is completely flat and matter-of-fact ('two minutes'). The LVAD battery setup from earlier pays off perfectly. Economy is flawless — one sentence, maximum impact. This is close to the highest anchor examples in compression and character specificity.

jokes.text: You guys do not like talking!
jokes.setup: Liz has just failed to get either Jack or Colleen to have an emotional conversation, and Colleen announced she might die rather than continue
jokes.punchline: Liz's exasperated understatement after a battery crisis/near-death scenario is deflating everything to the simplest observation
jokes.explanation: Good Liz reaction line. After the high absurdity of the battery/death sequence, her flat summation ('you guys do not like talking!') is a perfect deflation. The economy is excellent and it's quintessential Liz — observing obvious things with complete sincerity.

jokes.text: George Foreman is not going to Stanford. He's decided to permanently join the entourage. I'll start the paperwork. / It takes a week to get an I.D. / Tony will rush it for me. We do Zumba together.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces George Foreman won't go to college
jokes.punchline: The entourage has formal paperwork for membership, and Tracy's ID contact Tony is expedited through their Zumba relationship
jokes.explanation: The entourage bureaucracy is funny (paperwork, ID processing), and 'We do Zumba together' as a power connection is perfectly absurd for Tracy's world. The escalation of mundane details in an absurd setting works well.

jokes.text: Like teaching him how to ride a bike... Down the Luxor pyramid. / Or drive a car... into the ground. / I never even taught him how to shave... an orangutan.
jokes.setup: Tracy sadly lists all the father-son activities they never did
jokes.punchline: Each activity has a Tracy-specific twist: the bike is down a Las Vegas pyramid; the car driving is into franchise destruction; shaving is an orangutan — each completing the normal phrase with a chaotic Tracy addendum
jokes.explanation: Outstanding list joke. The structure is perfect: start a relatable father-son activity, then complete it with a Tracy-specific absurdity. Each entry escalates: Luxor pyramid (reckless but fun), franchise destruction (financial disaster), orangutan shaving (genuinely bizarre). The rhythm is impeccable — the pauses after each activity are crucial. Strong candidate for second-best joke in the episode. Very quotable.

jokes.text: You had the baby? Okay. Name him George Foreman. And also, we're out of soda at home.
jokes.setup: Tracy flashes back to the birth of George Foreman
jokes.punchline: He instructs Angie to name the baby 'George Foreman' and immediately follows up with a grocery note — treating childbirth as a brief to-do list item
jokes.explanation: Great Tracy joke. The phone call structure is perfect: naming a child AND grocery order in the same breath. 'We're out of soda at home' placed immediately after naming his newborn son is devastatingly funny and efficient. Strong Tracy character integration — he's simultaneously absent and weirdly domestic.

jokes.text: I wish I had a father to talk to. But Liz Lemon is the only person I know who even has a father. / Well, Mr. Jordan, speaking from experience, All My Children... was cancelled.
jokes.setup: Tracy wants parenting advice and notes Liz has a father
jokes.punchline: Dotcom offers to speak 'from experience' about fathers — but his reference is a cancelled soap opera, not personal experience, implying his father knowledge comes from 'All My Children'
jokes.explanation: Good multi-layer joke. First: Tracy's world is so celebrity-adjacent that Liz having a normal father is exotic. Second: Dotcom's 'from experience' pivot to a soap opera is a perfect Dotcom beat — he's the intellectual one who has nonetheless taken life lessons from daytime TV. The irony of 'All My Children was cancelled' as advice is perfect deadpan.

jokes.text: ♪ Mommy kangaroo mommy kangaroo / separate the races, mommy kangaroo ♪
jokes.setup: Russ's supposedly great new song plays
jokes.punchline: The children's kangaroo song suddenly includes 'separate the races' as a lyric — a horrific request buried in otherwise innocent children's song structure
jokes.explanation: Exceptional dark subversive joke. 'Separate the races, mommy kangaroo' is a perfectly horrifying line to include in a children's song — the rhyme and meter of the children's song format makes the racist request sound disturbingly sing-along-ready. The absurdity is that this is Jenna's boyfriend's 'great' song. The juxtaposition between the cute kangaroo song and apartheid-level ideology is devastating and very funny.

jokes.text: The what? / No. That song, like everything, is about me. I'm the baby kangaroo who went on the walkabout.
jokes.setup: Jenna has an emotional realization while listening to Russ's song and tells Russ she should go back to the Woggels
jokes.punchline: Russ thinks she means the Woggels, but Jenna clarifies that everything — including this kangaroo song — is actually about her. She's the baby kangaroo.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jenna characterization. Her narcissism is so total that a song written by someone else, about kangaroos, is somehow about her emotional journey. 'The what?' from Russ shows he's entirely lost, which amplifies Jenna's self-absorption. 'That song, like everything, is about me' is an excellent Jenna thesis statement.

jokes.text: Jack, can we make sure the pilot is a man. I don't know, ever since Amelia Earhart, I'm a little skittish about lady pilots. / Yes, mother, Captain Chuck Cutler. I'm told he has a mustache. / Mm, good.
jokes.setup: Colleen is preparing to leave; she has a pilot preference
jokes.punchline: Jack has already confirmed a male pilot with a mustache — and 'he has a mustache' is presented as a reassuring pilot credential. 'Mm, good.' confirms the mustache matters to Colleen.
jokes.explanation: Excellent exchange. The mustache as a pilot credential (confirming maleness beyond just the name 'Chuck') is the comedic peak. Jack playing along completely — pre-scouting the mustache situation — is both a great Jack detail and a sign of how well he knows Colleen's requirements. 'Mm, good.' is perfect as a final beat.

jokes.text: Sew up your cabbage hole, girl.
jokes.setup: Liz tries to get one more word in about Jack and Colleen having the talk
jokes.punchline: 'Sew up your cabbage hole' — an archaic, incomprehensible insult telling Liz to shut up, with 'cabbage hole' as a Victorian-era-sounding euphemism for mouth
jokes.explanation: One of the best Colleen lines ever. 'Cabbage hole' as a slang term for mouth is simultaneously archaic-sounding, vaguely Irish, and completely invented — yet it sounds like something that could be real. 'Sew up your cabbage hole' has the perfect rhythm and escalates 'shut your mouth' into something grotesque and specific. Extremely quotable. Colleen's vocabulary is the most distinctive on the show and this is a career highlight for the character.

jokes.text: Lime to a Lemon, you need to tell me what to do about George Foreman.
jokes.setup: Tracy approaches Liz for advice
jokes.punchline: 'Lime to a Lemon' as an address for Liz — Tracy's invented honorific that plays on her name while positioning himself as the lesser citrus
jokes.explanation: Fun Tracy wordplay. 'Lime to a Lemon' is a charming bit of Tracy-specific language that positions Liz as the authority while using fruit naming. It's unexpected and shows Tracy's odd creativity with names.

jokes.text: Three-way simultaneous conversation: Jenna ('Jenna made me forget about...why I came here'), Tracy ('What if I'm already too late?'), Liz Lemon ('What if Paul's actually...replaced me?') — all talking past each other.
jokes.setup: Three characters all urgently need Liz's advice at the same moment.
jokes.punchline: None of them listen to each other; they talk in overlapping fragments while Liz tries to mediate.
jokes.explanation: A structural comedy moment — the chaos of everyone needing advice simultaneously. Works as escalation and visual comedy but loses points for being more of a device than a specific joke.

jokes.text: Communicate! Go to Paul, go to George Foreman. And as difficult as it might be, talk to them. Before you lose them forever, tell them how you feel. Have the talk. George Foreman first, dinner break, then Paul.
jokes.setup: Liz gives a sincere speech about communication to Tracy and Jenna simultaneously
jokes.punchline: The speech goes from sincere emotional advice to logistical scheduling ('George Foreman first, dinner break, then Paul') — reducing emotional confrontations to a calendar
jokes.explanation: Good Liz joke. Her genuine emotional advice collapses into project management. 'Dinner break' is the key word — she's treating difficult emotional conversations as workday tasks with scheduled breaks. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, was that supposed to be for our benefit? Do you think we're idiots? / If you were my kid, I'd mail you back to the stork.
jokes.setup: Colleen and Jack overhear (or observe) Liz's speech and react
jokes.punchline: Jack's 'mail you back to the stork' as a child-rejection metaphor — upgrading 'send you back where you came from' into something both more absurd (storks aren't real) and more bureaucratic (via mail)
jokes.explanation: Sharp Jack line. 'Mail you back to the stork' has two great components: the stork mythology applied literally, and the postal method implying Jack/Colleen would formalize the rejection. The economy is excellent and it's very quotable. Shows both Donaghys united in dismissing Liz.

jokes.text: When I was eight, she took me to the post office because I spilled juice on a couch reserved for the Pope, which has still never been used. / He'll come.
jokes.setup: Jack confirms the 'mailing back' threat was real — Colleen tried to mail him as a child
jokes.punchline: Two jokes: (1) The couch was specifically reserved for the Pope. (2) 'He'll come' — Colleen still believes, decades later, that the Pope will visit and use the couch
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. The detail of a couch specifically reserved for the Pope is already perfect Colleen Catholicism (she has set aside furniture for a papal visit). But 'which has still never been used' and then Colleen's simple 'He'll come' — delivered with complete faith — is the best moment in this scene. It reveals Colleen's entire worldview: obsessive Catholicism, unshakeable conviction, and decades of patient furniture preservation. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: But I am sorry I tried to mail you. / I forgive you. And I'm sorry about the juice, which you should know was actually wine.
jokes.setup: Colleen apologizes for trying to mail 8-year-old Jack
jokes.punchline: Jack reveals the 'juice' was actually wine — he was drinking wine at age 8, which is both darker and funnier, and explains why Colleen was so upset (the Pope's couch defiled by child wine consumption)
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback escalation. The juice-was-wine reveal recontextualizes everything: Jack was drinking wine at 8, spilled it on papal furniture, and still frames it as 'juice' in his apology (a lingering instinct to hide it). The Donaghy childhood dysfunction deepens with each beat. The apology/forgiveness structure becoming a confessional of further crimes is excellent construction.

jokes.text: You know, you've always been my favorite child. / Thank you. / You never gave me any trouble. You always ate your vegetables, you went to church, and you loved breast feeding.
jokes.setup: Colleen finally says something warm — Jack is her favorite
jokes.punchline: The reasons she lists escalate from reasonable (no trouble, vegetables) to weird (church) to uncomfortable and overshared ('loved breast feeding') — the list ending on an intimate detail destroys the warmth
jokes.explanation: Good escalating list joke in the Colleen tradition. The pivot from touching to awkward is well-timed — 'loved breast feeding' as the final item in a list of Jack's virtues is both inappropriate and funny, especially because Colleen delivers it with the same weight as 'ate your vegetables.' The moment where Jack's apparent sincerity gets deflated by his mother's oversharing is very funny.

jokes.text: If I've ever had any success in this life, it's because of you. / Oh. / I made this happen!
jokes.setup: Jack has a genuine emotional moment with Colleen
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately takes credit for brokering the emotional moment — loudly, from the doorway
jokes.explanation: Good Liz beat. The intrusion on a genuinely touching moment with 'I made this happen!' deflates the emotion perfectly and is very in-character. The staging — Liz observing from outside and crashing in — is classic 30 Rock structure.

jokes.text: Not a part of this, I get it. But I made this happen! I made this happen.
jokes.setup: Jack and Colleen ignore Liz and continue their moment
jokes.punchline: Liz is shut out of the emotional reconciliation she engineered and responds by repeating her credit-taking twice more — getting louder each time
jokes.explanation: Good sustained Liz beat. Being frozen out of the moment she created and insisting on credit anyway is very Liz. The repetition escalating slightly in volume/desperation is a good running gag structure. Works better as physical comedy with Tina Fey's performance.

jokes.text: Son, this isn't easy for me to say, because my tongue caught what my foot has.
jokes.setup: Tracy has a serious conversation with George Foreman
jokes.punchline: 'My tongue caught what my foot has' — Tracy's version of 'tongue-tied,' implying his tongue has a foot disease (fungus? injury?), delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tracy malapropism/invented idiom. 'My tongue caught what my foot has' is a masterclass in Tracy-speak — it's trying to say 'tongue-tied' but arrives somewhere much weirder, implying cross-body disease transmission. The earnestness of the delivery makes it land. Very quotable and extremely character-specific.

jokes.text: Even if you become a doctor, or a lawyer, or a philanthropist who devotes his life to others. I'll still be proud of you.
jokes.setup: Tracy promises to be proud of George Foreman no matter what path he chooses
jokes.punchline: Tracy lists respectable careers in ascending order of nobility, treating 'philanthropist who devotes his life to others' as the worst possible outcome — all delivered with grimly sincere acceptance
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Tracy's escalating list of 'acceptable' outcomes ends with selfless philanthropy framed as the hardest thing to accept. His 'I'll still be proud of you' implies this last option would truly test his love. Excellent character integration — Tracy views public service as alien and somewhat embarrassing.

jokes.text: Good-bye, my son. / But dad, college doesn't start for another five months. / I said, good-bye, my son.
jokes.setup: Tracy says a dramatic farewell to George Foreman as if he's leaving forever
jokes.punchline: George Foreman points out college is months away; Tracy repeats his dramatic farewell anyway — committing to the theatrical goodbye regardless of practical timeline
jokes.explanation: Perfect Tracy beat. He's committed to the emotional farewell and refuses to let facts interrupt it. 'I said, good-bye, my son' — the 'I said' repeating it with royal finality despite the five-month reality check — is great character work. The pathos-comedy balance is well-executed.

jokes.text: Oh, God. He's dressed like her.
jokes.setup: Jenna arrives to win Paul back and finds he has been replaced
jokes.punchline: Paul's replacement is dressed identically to Jenna — a visual gag implying Paul found an exact Jenna substitute, and they went all the way to matching outfits
jokes.explanation: Strong visual gag that works even without seeing the image. 'He's dressed like her' as a three-word horror reveal is efficient and funny. The implication — Paul has found a perfect Jenna substitute complete with outfit — is both absurd and a sharp commentary on Jenna/Paul's relationship dynamics. Rewatch bonus for the actual visual.

jokes.text: Look on the bright side. My thing went perfectly.
jokes.setup: Jenna's relationship has collapsed; Paul has replaced her
jokes.punchline: Liz's comfort is to note her unrelated professional accomplishment — she's not consoling Jenna, she's redirecting to herself
jokes.explanation: Good Liz moment. Her 'comfort' for Jenna is completely self-referential — in a moment of Jenna's genuine heartbreak, Liz pivots to her own success. The obliviousness is very Liz, and the economy of the delivery ('My thing went perfectly') is a good button.

jokes.text: This was your mother's. / Well, I know, but I wanted to make sure you got it. // Hang on. If your plan was to have surgery, then go back to Florida without ever seeing me, why did you bring this with you?
jokes.setup: Colleen gives Jack a keepsake — implying she always planned to see him
jokes.punchline: Jack realizes Colleen's 'insurance excuse' for being in New York was always a lie — she brought a personal keepsake, which you don't do if you're not planning to see someone
jokes.explanation: More of a character/plot beat than a pure joke, but the irony of Colleen being caught in her pretense of not wanting to see Jack — via the keepsake evidence — is well-constructed. The comedy is in Jack's detective-mode realization and Colleen's subsequent flustering.

jokes.text: What is this, the Spanish Inquisition? / Oh. Oh, you'd know. You lived through it.
jokes.setup: Colleen deflects Jack's question with 'What is this, the Spanish Inquisition?'
jokes.punchline: Jack points out that Colleen is old enough to have actually lived through the Spanish Inquisition — a joke about her extreme age delivered as a calm factual correction
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke structure. The 'Spanish Inquisition' idiom is typically safe because no one literally experienced it. Jack's pivot ('you'd know, you lived through it') is perfectly timed and lands well as both an age joke and a commentary on Colleen's ancientness. 'Oh.' as his beat before delivering it is great timing.

jokes.text: Get...off. Ow! / Get...off. / I did this!
jokes.setup: Jack and Colleen share a hug (presumably awkward given their relationship)
jokes.punchline: Liz crashes their hug and they both resist her while she insists on credit again ('I did this!')
jokes.explanation: Third 'I did this!' callback, now with physical comedy as Liz forces herself into the hug. Works as a capper to the running gag and is better as physical comedy (seeing Tina Fey get pushed away while yelling credit). The escalation from verbal credit-taking to forcing herself into the hug is a good arc.

jokes.text: Final Woggels song: '♪ Apples / you taste good / Trees / you give us wood / Grandma / I am gay / Bridge / you turn me on in a sexual way ♪'
jokes.setup: The Woggels (now with Russ back) perform their reformed children's show.
jokes.punchline: The list song escalates from wholesome ('apples / you taste good') to increasingly inappropriate: grandma being gay, bridges being sexually arousing.
jokes.explanation: A perfect closing joke for the Woggels arc. The list structure (established in the opening Woggels songs) now delivers two escalating inappropriate revelations. 'Grandma / I am gay' is a great setup, but 'Bridge / you turn me on in a sexual way' is the true punchline. The structure — normal things, then these — pays off the running gag beautifully. One of the episode's strongest jokes.

jokes.text: ♪ Apples / You taste good / Trees / You give us wood / Grandma / I am gay / Bridge / You turn me on in a sexual way ♪
jokes.setup: The Woggels close the episode with a song in call-and-response format
jokes.punchline: The children's song escalates from innocent ('apples / you taste good') to a grandma announcing her sexuality to inappropriate sexual feelings about infrastructure ('bridge / you turn me on in a sexual way')
jokes.explanation: Outstanding closing joke. The escalation is perfectly calibrated: apples/taste good (innocent), trees/give us wood ('wood' double entendre sneaking in), grandma/I am gay (sudden character confession — grandma is coming out in a children's song), bridge/turns me on sexually (infrastructure attraction). The structure is brilliant — each pairing gets progressively more inappropriate while maintaining the cheerful call-and-response format. 'You turn me on in a sexual way' about a bridge is the perfect ending for a 30 Rock Woggels episode. Comparable to the highest-tier anchor examples in construction and originality.

tmdb_overview: Jack's mom upstages his ribbon-cutting ceremony. Meanwhile Jenna hooks up with a "rock star" and Tracy frets about his son heading to college.
insight: Absurdist humor dominates 87.6-rated episode with 2.32 jokes-per-minute velocity.
